section_1.title: Prerequisite Warm-up: The Shape of Certainty
section_1.content: Briefly define a Normal Distribution (Gaussian) by its two parameters: mean (μ) representing the center, and variance (σ²) representing the 'spread' or 'noise'. Introduce the visual representation as a symmetrical 'Bell Curve'.
section_1.example: Imagine a robot cat fetching snacks; the time it takes follows a Bell Curve centered at 5 minutes.

section_2.title: The Problem: Adding Two Independent Random Variables
section_2.content: Pose the question: If we have two independent sources of random noise, what happens when we combine them? Visually represent two distinct Bell Curves moving toward each other and merging into one.
section_2.example: A cat walks to the kitchen (X ~ N(μ1, σ1²)) and then spends time hunting for a toy (Y ~ N(μ2, σ2²)). How do we describe the total time (X + Y)?

section_3.title: The Rule: Summation of Parameters
section_3.content: Explain the elegant result: The sum remains Gaussian. The new mean is the sum of the means (μ_new = μ1 + μ2), and the new variance is the sum of the variances (σ²_new = σ1² + σ2²). Emphasize that variances add, not standard deviations.
section_3.example: If the cat's travel time is N(5, 1) and hunting time is N(3, 2), the total time is N(5+3, 1+2), which is N(8, 3).

section_4.title: Visualizing the 'Broadening'
section_4.content: Display an animation where two narrow bell curves combine to form a wider, taller bell curve. Explain that because variances are additive, uncertainty always increases when you add independent sources of randomness.
section_4.example: Visual overlay of the two initial narrow peaks transforming into one flattened, wider peak representing the final total duration.

section_5.title: Summary & Real-World Application
section_5.content: Recap the core takeaway: Summing independent Gaussians is mathematically 'closed'—the result never escapes the Gaussian family. Mention applications in error propagation in engineering or finance.
section_5.example: In sensor fusion, combining GPS noise (Gaussian) with IMU noise (Gaussian) results in a total system error that is still a predictable, measurable Gaussian Bell Curve.

section_2.title: The Problem: Adding Two Independent Random Variables
section_2.content: Pose the question: If we have two independent sources of random noise, what happens when we combine them? Visually represent two distinct Bell Curves moving toward each other and merging into one.
section_2.example: A cat walks to the kitchen (X ~ N(μ1, σ1²)) and then spends time hunting for a toy (Y ~ N(μ2, σ2²)). How do we describe the total time (X + Y)?

section_3.title: The Rule: Summation of Parameters
section_3.content: Explain the elegant result: The sum remains Gaussian. The new mean is the sum of the means (μ_new = μ1 + μ2), and the new variance is the sum of the variances (σ²_new = σ1² + σ2²). Emphasize that variances add, not standard deviations.
section_3.example: If the cat's travel time is N(5, 1) and hunting time is N(3, 2), the total time is N(5+3, 1+2), which is N(8, 3).

section_4.title: Visualizing the 'Broadening'
section_4.content: Display an animation where two narrow bell curves combine to form a wider, taller bell curve. Explain that because variances are additive, uncertainty always increases when you add independent sources of randomness.
section_4.example: Visual overlay of the two initial narrow peaks transforming into one flattened, wider peak representing the final total duration.

section_5.title: Summary & Real-World Application
section_5.content: Recap the core takeaway: Summing independent Gaussians is mathematically 'closed'—the result never escapes the Gaussian family. Mention applications in error propagation in engineering or finance.
section_5.example: In sensor fusion, combining GPS noise (Gaussian) with IMU noise (Gaussian) results in a total system error that is still a predictable, measurable Gaussian Bell Curve.
